title: Harmonic Burst Mesh — stress sweep & priming matrix (scratch)
content:
Context and goal:
- Trying a different angle on surge interference: instead of single long bursts, create a harmonic mesh of staggered sinusoidal QPS waves from many small clients. Hypothesis: overlapping phase offsets create persistent micro-resonance that degrades tail latency more than equivalent Poisson bursts.
- Also testing cache priming strategies (prefix-only vs full-KV priming) to see if small priming investments reduce p99 under mesh patterns.

Environment:
- Cluster: dev-fleet-gpu-12 (8x A10g), serving-runtime branch: harmonic-mesh-2025, kernel tuning flag: fastpath-attenuation=true
- Model: rwd-open-3b-quant (seq_len 2048), kv-cache enabled
- Clients: 64 synthetic clients, each generates sin(qps_base + amplitude * sin(2π * freq * t + phase))
- QPS baseline: 0.8 -> burst peaks to 6.0 per client (effective aggregate peak ~384 qps)
- Phases: uniformly distributed [0, 2π], freq sweep: 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 Hz (periods 20s, 10s, 5s)
- Run lengths: 15m per sweep, warmup: 3m steady low qps before each run

Experiment matrix (short):
- Priming modes: none, prefix-only (first 256 tokens), full-KV (send short warm-up requests to populate entire KV for common contexts)
- Client wave coherence: uniform-phase, clustered-phase (4 clusters with near-identical phases), synchronized (all same phase)
- Cache hit-rate target (observed): low (<5%), medium (30-50%), high (>70%) depending on priming intensity and working set

Metrics collected:
- p50/p95/p99 generation latency (server-side), request QPS, KV cache hit %, GPU util, seq length distribution, queue depth distribution
- Additional: token emission rate, tail retry counts, aborts, and backpressure events

Representative run notes (2025-06-11):
1) Sweep freq=0.1Hz, uniform-phase, no priming
- Aggregate mean qps: 270 (oscillates 120 -> 384)
- KV hit %: 6%
- p50: 82ms, p95: 310ms, p99: 1.38s
- Observations: frequent short queuing spikes, GPU util climbs to 95% near peaks, small windowed preemption delays cause long tails. Queue depths spike in 100-150ms windows.
- Quick chart refs: [chart: runA_freq01_noPriming_qps_vs_p99.png]

2) Sweep freq=0.1Hz, uniform-phase, prefix-only priming
- Aggregate mean qps: 265
- KV hit %: 28%
- p50: 74ms, p95: 260ms, p99: 780ms
- Observations: clear improvement at p99 (~45% reduction). Implication: even short prefix priming helps KV reuse across overlapping requests. However memory pressure increases ~6% and occasional eviction events seen.

3) Sweep freq=0.1Hz, clustered-phase (4 clusters), prefix-only priming
- Aggregate mean qps: 280
- KV hit %: 34% (within clusters sharing contexts)
- p50: 78ms, p95: 290ms, p99: 1.05s
- Observations: clustering created higher local peaks and more synchronized short bursts inside each cluster -> tail got worse vs uniform-phase with same priming. So phase distribution matters: clustered-phase reduces cross-client cache benefits when clusters mismatch working sets.

4) Sweep freq=0.05Hz (longer period), synchronized phase, full-KV priming
- Aggregate mean qps: 240
- KV hit %: 74%
- p50: 68ms, p95: 220ms, p99: 420ms
- Observations: best tail results so far. Full-KV priming expensive but effective when client waves are synchronized: reuse is maximal, GPU kernels operate at better batching efficiencies. Trade-off: warmup priming cost ~1.8x tokens for 30s, acceptable if surge duration >60s.

5) High-frequency mesh (freq=0.2Hz), uniform-phase, prefix-only
- KV hit %: 18%
- p50: 96ms, p95: 420ms, p99: 1.9s
- Observations: fast oscillations create many short-lived overlapping queues; batching can't coalesce well because phase changes faster than batch window. Tail degrades significantly.

6) Control: Poisson arrivals matched to same mean qps as case 1
- p50: 80ms, p95: 290ms, p99: 620ms
- Observations: Poisson tails are noticeably better than harmonic mesh no-priming (p99 1.38s -> 620ms). Confirms hypothesis: harmonic interference is worse for tail.

Key takeaways (rough):
- Harmonic mesh patterns produce higher p99 than Poisson at similar mean qps, especially at medium frequencies (0.1Hz) and with unprimed caches.
- Small prefix priming (256 tokens) delivers big wins (30–50% p99 reduction) for uniform-phase traffic at moderate frequencies, with modest memory overhead.
- Full-KV priming is most effective when client waves are synchronized or when working sets are small and common, but its token cost must be amortized across surge duration.
- Clustered-phase setups can defeat priming benefits if clusters have disjoint working sets. Cache priming strategy should be coupled with clustering detection.
- Fast oscillations (freq >=0.2Hz) reduce batching/coalescing efficiency; consider adaptive batch windows or micro-throttle.

Action items / next experiments:
- Implement micro-batching window adaptation: widen batch window by 10–30ms when detect high-frequency oscillations; measure impact on p95/p99 vs latency inflation.
- Add client-side context hashing to correlate similar contexts and route those to the same warm-up lane (experiment: expedite cache sharing).
- Cost calc: run an economic simulation for full-KV priming (token cost vs p99 reduction) for surge durations 30s/60s/180s.
- Add metric: eviction churn rate and per-GPU KV occupancy timeline to correlate with p99 spikes.

Open questions / hypotheses to validate:
- Is there a sweet-spot frequency range where prefix-only priming is most cost-effective? (Initial result: around 0.05–0.12Hz seems promising)
- Can an opportunistic priming policy (only prime when predicted surge > threshold) get most of the benefit with less token cost?
- Does serving-runtime kernel scheduling contribute to long tails during short micro-peaks? Need trace-level correlation with kernel stalls.

Notes to self: stash these baseline logs -> CON-1287, attach runA/B/C artifacts, capture flame graphs for 2025-06-11 10:00-10:20 window. Ping SRE (Liam) about eviction tuning. Walk Priya through cluster-phase experiments tomorrow.

Quick summary (one-liner for Slack):
"Harmonic mesh bursts hurt p99 significantly; lightweight prefix priming recovers a lot of tail, full-KV priming wins when waves synchronize — tradeoffs: token cost and eviction churn. Next: adaptive batching + opportunistic priming tests."

- A, 0.10, uniform, none, 6, 82, 310, 1380
- B, 0.10, uniform, prefix, 28, 74, 260, 780
- C, 0.10, clustered, prefix, 34, 78, 290, 1050

- E, 0.20, uniform, prefix, 18, 96, 420, 1900

End of scratch notes.
